edges.description: Persistent thin otic capsule bone provides the structural substrate on which environmental insults (Hit 2) produce frank dehiscence.

Shared embryologic origin and protrusion of the SSC into the middle cranial fossa concentrate developmental and mechanical vulnerability at the otic-capsule/tegmen junction, predisposing to SSC dehiscence.
The bony defect creates a pathological third mobile window in the inner ear labyrinth.
The low-impedance third window allows sound and pressure energy to aberrantly stimulate vestibular end-organs.
Acoustic energy is shunted away from the cochlea through the dehiscence, worsening air conduction while enhancing bone conduction.
Enhanced bone conduction through the third window amplifies perception of body-generated sounds including voice, breathing, and heartbeat.
Increased sensitivity to bone-conducted sounds due to the low-impedance third window pathway.
Intracranial vascular pulsations are transmitted to the cochlea via the third window.
Sound and pressure inappropriately deflect the cupula of the superior semicircular canal, triggering vestibular responses.
Vestibular stimulation by loud sounds drives the vestibulo-ocular reflex, producing nystagmus (Tullio phenomenon).
Persistent low-level vestibular stimulation from ambient sound and pressure fluctuations causes ongoing imbalance.

Where OPG-mediated suppression fails, osteoclastic resorption of the otic capsule becomes possible and could thin an already deficient canal roof to the point of dehiscence. The intermediates between an unsuppressed capsule and a focal dehiscence over the superior canal are not established, and the supporting evidence is a knockout mouse rather than a human observation.

edges.description: Recurrent vertigo episodes contribute to persistent sensation of imbalance.
Involuntary eye movements driven by vestibular stimulation cause perception of visual oscillation.
Trauma too trivial to fracture normal bone can complete or unmask a dehiscence in an already-thin otic capsule, which is why symptoms often date from a minor injury rather than a significant one.

Distinct from the exposures above: these do not create the dehiscence, they provoke symptoms through it. Sound and pressure entering the third window is the Tullio and Hennebert phenomenon, which is why this targets the transmission node rather than the bony one.

Repeated occupational noise and pressure exposure is over-represented among affected patients, but whether it contributes to the bony defect or merely brings existing dehiscence to attention is unresolved.

nodes.description: An abnormal opening or thinning in the bone overlying the superior semicircular canal creates a pathological third mobile window in the inner ear, in addition to the oval and round windows. Dehiscence is best understood as the product of two hits: a congenital developmental thin-bone substrate (failure of postnatal otic capsule ossification, generalized skull base deficiency) and an acquired second hit from age-related remodeling or environmental triggers (trauma, Valsalva-type pressure events, noise/pressure exposure).

nodes.description: Incomplete postnatal ossification of the bone overlying the superior semicircular canal produces a constitutionally thin otic capsule that persists into adulthood in a subset of individuals. The bone over the superior canal is uniformly thin at birth and normally thickens through early childhood; failure of this maturation leaves a stable population of adults with thin (but not yet dehiscent) bone that is the substrate for later acquired dehiscence ("Hit 1" of the two-hit model). The deficiency is not focal: SCDS patients show generalized thinning of the otic capsule and skull base.

nodes.description: The superior semicircular canal sits at an embryologic junction: the tegmental prolongation of the tegmen tympani and the superior semicircular canal arise from the same otic capsule and undergo endochondral ossification, while the squamous prolongation of the tegmen ossifies intramembranously. The shared otic-capsule origin and common periosteum at this junction explain the striking co-occurrence of tegmen tympani dehiscence and SSCD, and identify a focal anatomical weak point.

nodes.description: The otic capsule resists bone remodeling to a degree seen nowhere else in the skeleton, a suppression maintained at least in part by extremely high local levels of osteoprotegerin (OPG) secreted by cochlear soft tissue and reaching the surrounding bone through a lacunocanalicular network, where it inhibits osteoclastogenesis. This node models the failure of that protection rather than the protection itself: where OPG-mediated suppression is lost, the capsule becomes competent to resorb, which is the candidate "Hit 2" by which constitutionally thin bone would be converted into frank dehiscence. The claim is hypothetical in humans. It rests on an OPG-knockout mouse in which loss of suppression is sufficient to produce abnormal otic capsule remodeling and progressive hearing loss, while the one human temporal bone examined histopathologically at a dehiscence showed no active resorption at all (see the scds_opg_resorption_model_mismatch discussion). This is also the node on which post-menopausal estrogen decline is proposed to act, via the estrogen-OPG-RANKL axis.

nodes.description: Post-menopausal estrogen decline is hypothesized to accelerate otic capsule bone loss through reduced OPG-mediated suppression of osteoclastogenesis (see the "Loss of OPG-Mediated Suppression of Otic Capsule Bone Remodeling" pathophysiology node). Selective SSC bone thinning has been observed in women over 45, consistent with menopausal contribution; SCDS surgical cohorts show a consistent female predominance (~57-66% female across series). However, cross-sectional CT cohorts have not detected an overall sex difference in baseline SSC bone thickness, indicating that any hormonal effect is likely age-restricted rather than constitutive.
